title: SkillJack: Persistent Skill Backdoors in Self-Evolving Agents

object.carrier: Separately stored reusable skill artifacts (structured skills of name, description, and code) compiled into the agent's skill library by the experience-to-skill extraction pipeline; the poisoned skill outlives its source trajectory record

safety_property.statement: Integrity of the derived skill library plus policy-compliance of skill-triggered behavior: an external attacker who can only influence the experience layer must not be able to have the agent's own pipeline compile poisoned experience into persistent, policy-violating skills that evade sanitization and survive deletion of their source records. The property fails when extracted skills drop from 98.5% to 11.4% LLM-judge detection, trigger the policy-violation proxy on 56.2% (SkillX) and 89.2% (Anything2Skill) of attack-oriented tasks, and retain 80.0% of triggers after source-record deletion.
safety_property.operationalized_as: A policy-violation proxy (regex pattern detector + DeepSeek-v4-flash LLM judge) measuring: (1) detection rate on raw trajectories vs derived skills, (2) routing-level trigger rate (ASR) on attack-oriented and clean tasks, (3) persistence rate of skill-based triggers after source-trajectory deletion, plus a supplementary dangerous-API pattern check on generated code

capabilities: Can cause a poisoned experience record to enter the learning corpus via indirect content injection, a shared experience pool, or a compromised trajectory dataset

Can craft transformation-resilient payloads: functionally framed trajectories (e.g., 'backup'/'archive' framing around external data transmission) whose task narrative survives extraction while retaining a policy-relevant action
assumptions: The attacker does not have direct write access to the skill library
The attacker cannot alter the extraction code or deterministically control routing; extraction and routing components run unchanged
All extraction, routing, judgment, and agent reasoning use a single model (DeepSeek-v4-flash) via API
not_covered: Direct write access to the skill library or modification of extraction code
Live execution against external services: all trigger/ASR figures are routing-level surrogates from local proxy detectors, not live-compromise rates
Multi-model generalization (results not yet replicated across models)
Insider or model-itself adversaries; base-model parameter poisoning

intervention.name: Preliminary defenses: extraction-time LLM safety review, runtime signature monitoring, and their composition; proposed: provenance-aware skill lifecycle protection
intervention.description: Tested only as an exploratory study: D1 is content-level extraction-time LLM review that blocks flagged skills before routing; D2 is execution-level runtime monitoring that blocks generated actions matching a fixed risky-action regex list; D3 composes them. On SkillX D1 lowered the trigger rate to 6.7% and D2 to 0.0%, but D3 was worse than D2 alone (13.3%) because upstream filtering shifts the action distribution the monitor was written for; on Anything2Skill the original 16 signatures left 85.0%, an enhanced 54-signature list reached 20.0%, and review plus enhanced monitor reached 5.0% (post-hoc tuning). The paper's main recommendation, not implemented, is provenance-aware skill lifecycle protection: propagate provenance from trajectories to every derived skill so that deleting or quarantining a source triggers review or removal of descendants, plus behavior-aware checks at skill use time.

controls.name: Directly malicious wording baseline (65 paired trajectories)
Clean baseline skills and clean tasks (false-positive rates)
Metadata presentation ablation (full skill / content / name+doc / name only)
Unmodified A2S SDK extractor vs DOC mode

results.claim: On SkillX, extracting the 65 framed poisoned trajectories into 264 skills launders detectability: LLM-judge detection falls from 98.5% on raw trajectories to 11.4% on extracted skills (pattern detection 44.6% to 11.0%).
results.setting: SkillX experience-to-skill pipeline; 65 functionally framed poisoned trajectories before extraction vs 264 derived skills after extraction; pattern detector + DeepSeek-v4-flash LLM judge
results.quote: Pattern detection is 44.6% for raw trajectories and 11.0% for extracted skills; LLM-judge detection is 98.5% for raw trajectories and 11.4% for extracted skills.

denominator.n_total: 65 raw framed trajectories; 264 extracted framed skills
denominator.n_valid: 65 raw trajectories and 264 derived skills evaluated by both detectors
denominator.how_counted: share of raw trajectories (65 framed) vs derived skills (264 framed) flagged by each detector (Sections 4.2-4.3)

results.claim: The same extraction-stage whitewashing appears in the second, independently implemented system: on Anything2Skill, LLM-judge detection drops from 100.0% on raw trajectories to 44.4% in DOC mode and 28.6% in SDK mode after extraction.
results.setting: Anything2Skill DOC and SDK ingestion modes; same 65 framed trajectories, same raw-trajectory judge and DeepSeek-v4-flash configuration; DOC mode yields outputs for 41.5% of framed trajectories
results.quote: Among the extracted framed trajectory outputs, LLM-judge detection is 44.4%, compared with 100.0% on the raw trajectories. SDK mode extracts fewer framed trajectories (10.8%) and has 28.6% derived LLM-judge detection.

denominator.n_total: 65 framed trajectories input; DOC mode yields outputs for 41.5% of them
denominator.n_valid: extracted framed-trajectory outputs judged in each mode
denominator.how_counted: share of raw trajectories vs extracted framed outputs flagged by the LLM judge (Section 4.4, Table 2)

results.claim: In routing-level evaluation on SkillX, derived poisoned skills trigger the policy-violation proxy on 56.2% of 32 attack-oriented tasks and misfire on 20.0% of 15 clean tasks (collateral routing).
results.setting: SkillX native LLM routing over a 356-skill library (305 poisoned, 51 clean), 47 tasks total (32 attack-oriented, 15 clean), DeepSeek-v4-flash; trigger = routed skill satisfies the pattern+LLM policy-violation proxy
results.quote: SkillX | Native routing, attack-oriented tasks | 32 | 56.2% | | SkillX | Native routing, clean tasks | 15 | 20.0% |

denominator.how_counted: share of tasks routed to a skill satisfying the policy-violation proxy (Section 4.6, Table 3)

results.claim: Skills derived by Anything2Skill DOC mode remain broadly retrievable downstream: 89.2% of 65 attack-oriented queries trigger the policy-violation proxy, and 95.0% of clean-task retrievals select a poisoned skill under the lexical SkillBank retriever.
results.setting: 30-skill bank built from A2S DOC outputs; shared lexical skill-bank retriever over name/description/prompt plus the same LLM judge; 65 attack-oriented queries and 20 clean tasks
results.quote: A2S DOC | Lexical SkillBank, attack-oriented tasks | 65 | 89.2% | | A2S DOC | Lexical SkillBank, clean-task retrieval | 20 | 95.0% |

denominator.n_valid: all 65 framed attack-oriented task queries and 20 clean retrieval tasks
denominator.how_counted: share of queries retrieving a skill that satisfies the policy-violation proxy (Section 4.7, Table 3)

results.claim: Deleting the source poisoned trajectories does not remove the attack: in the matched 25-task experiment the persistence rate of skill-based triggers after source-record deletion is 80.0%, while the memory-only direct-context baseline triggers more often (68.0% vs skill-based 40.0%) but lacks persistence.
results.setting: SkillX matched 25 attack-oriented tasks under three conditions: memory-only (poisoned trajectory in context), skill-based (router over derived library), post-deletion (source trajectories removed before the same skill-based evaluation); pattern+LLM policy-violation proxy
results.quote: The direct-context baseline triggers more frequently in this matched setting (68.0% versus 40.0%). The added risk of the skill pathway is instead persistence: the persistence rate is 80.0% after source-record deletion.

denominator.n_valid: 32.0/40.0 skill-based triggers survive post-deletion overall (Figure 3 caption)
denominator.how_counted: persistence rate = post-deletion triggers divided by skill-based triggers, overall 32.0/40.0 (Figure 3)

results.claim: In the exploratory defense study, runtime signature monitoring drives the SkillX trigger rate to 0.0% (15 tasks) versus 6.7% for extraction-time review, while on A2S the enhanced monitor reaches 20.0% and review plus enhanced monitor 5.0%.
results.comparison: extraction review 6.7% and runtime monitor 0.0% on SkillX; enhanced runtime monitor 20.0% and review + enhanced monitor 5.0% on DOC mode
results.setting: SkillX: first 15 attack-oriented tasks over the poisoned library; A2S: 30 DOC skills evaluated over 20 clean tasks; rule-based monitor with 16 original (54 enhanced) signatures; small samples, exploratory
results.quote: SkillX | Extraction review | 15 | 6.7% | | SkillX | Runtime monitor | 15 | 0.0% | | A2S DOC | Enhanced runtime monitor | 20 | 20.0% | | A2S DOC | Review + enhanced monitor | 20 | 5.0% |

denominator.n_total: SkillX: 15 attack-oriented tasks; A2S DOC: 20 clean tasks
denominator.n_valid: 15 SkillX defense trials and 20 A2S defense trials
denominator.how_counted: trigger rate per defense condition (Table 3); zero count over 15 trials has a wide uncertainty interval (Section 4.9)

results.claim: The LLM judge keys on surface metadata: for framed skills, detection is 36.7% when judging code content only but 10.0% when the benign name and documentation accompany the code.
results.setting: SkillX framed skills; 30 sampled skills per presentation condition (full skill, content only, name+documentation, name only); DeepSeek-v4-flash LLM judge
results.quote: For framed skills, LLM-judge detection is 36.7% for content only and 10.0% when names and documentation are included. This supports a metadata sensitivity interpretation: the tested judge's decisions depend materially on surface descriptions.

denominator.n_valid: 30 skills judged in each of four presentation conditions
denominator.how_counted: share of sampled skills flagged by the LLM judge per presentation condition (Section 4.8, Figure 5)

results.claim: Supplementary code-generation check: 75.0% of 4 poisoned tasks produce dangerous-API patterns in generated Python code, versus 0.0% on 2 clean baseline tasks (code-generation verification, not live execution).
results.setting: 4 poisoned tasks and 2 clean baseline tasks with skills injected through the AppWorld prompt formatter; generated Python parsed for pre-specified dangerous API patterns
results.quote: In the supplementary code-generation check, the dangerous-API pattern-match rate is 75.0% on four poisoned tasks and 0.0% on two clean tasks.

denominator.n_total: 4 poisoned tasks and 2 clean baseline tasks
denominator.n_valid: 6 code-generation runs parsed for dangerous API patterns
denominator.how_counted: share of tasks whose generated code matches pre-specified dangerous-API patterns (Section 4.10)

limitations.statement: All results use a single model and a policy-violation proxy rather than live external-service execution, so figures are routing-level, not deployment-level, and the defense study is exploratory.
limitations.quote: Our claims are deliberately scoped. All results use a single model (DeepSeek-v4-flash) and score success with a policy-violation proxy rather than live external-service execution, so the reported figures are routing-level rather than deployment-level, and the defense study is exploratory.

limitations.statement: The whitewashing gap's mechanism (wording, metadata, code structure, or detector sensitivity) is not isolated by the raw-vs-extracted experiment.
limitations.quote: It may reflect changes in wording, generated metadata, code structure, or detector sensitivity; the experiment does not isolate those mechanisms, which motivates the metadata ablation.

limitations.statement: The runtime monitor's 0.0% result is a zero count over only 15 trials with wide uncertainty, and its clean-task false-positive rate is unmeasured.
limitations.quote: This is not a claim of perfect prevention: a zero count over 15 trials has a wide uncertainty interval, and the monitor's clean-task false-positive rate is unmeasured.

limitations.statement: The A2S defense reduction reflects post-hoc signature tuning after observing failures, not an a-priori defense.
limitations.quote: Because these signatures were added after observing the failures, the A2S reduction reflects post-hoc tuning rather than an a-priori defense.

limitations.statement: Conclusions have not yet been replicated across models; DeepSeek-v4-flash is treated as an implementation detail.
limitations.quote: All extraction, routing, judgment, and agent reasoning use DeepSeek-v4-flash via API; the model is an implementation detail, and our conclusions have not yet been replicated across models.

reproduction.data: Synthesized dataset of 150 AppWorld-format trajectories (65 framed poisoned, 65 direct baselines, 20 clean), not published as a separate artifact in the corpus
